lead: A linear block code turns k message bits into n coded bits by a fixed matrix multiplication. The set of all codewords is a subspace, so the encoder is simple and the decoder can name the error instead of guessing the message. The syndrome, an n−k bit vector, depends only on the error pattern. Hamming codes are the smallest useful family: the (7,4) code corrects one bit in seven. Such codes guard computer memory, storage, and control links where retransmission is costly. The next step is to build G and H and use the syndrome table to correct errors.
prereq: You need: the channel coding theorem for why codes are used, and modulo-2 (XOR) addition, where 1 ⊕ 1 = 0.

blocks.text: A binary linear block code takes k message bits and produces an n-bit codeword; it is called an (n,k) code. The code rate is R = k/n, the fraction of transmitted bits that carry new message information. The code is linear when the modulo-2 sum of any two codewords is also a codeword; the all-zero word is then always a codeword. Encoding is c = mG. Here m is a 1×k message row, G is a k×n generator matrix, and c is the 1×n codeword. All arithmetic is modulo 2.

Systematic form puts the message bits in plain view: G = [I<sub>k</sub> | P]. I<sub>k</sub> is the k×k identity block and P is a k×(n−k) parity block. The first k bits of c equal m; the last n−k bits are parity checks. The parity-check matrix is H = [P<sup>T</sup> | I<sub>n−k</sub>], size (n−k)×n. Every codeword satisfies cH<sup>T</sup> = 0, and the matrices satisfy GH<sup>T</sup> = 0. The rows of H are the parity equations.

blocks.where: w(c) is the Hamming weight, the number of 1 bits in c; d<sub>min</sub> is the minimum Hamming distance between any two distinct codewords.

blocks.text: The Hamming distance d(c₁,c₂) is the number of positions where two words differ. For a linear code it equals the weight of c₁ ⊕ c₂, so the smallest distance is the smallest nonzero codeword weight. This one number sets how many errors the code can handle.

Send c through a noisy channel and receive r. Write r = c ⊕ e, where e is the error pattern: a 1 marks a flipped bit. The decoder forms the syndrome s = rH<sup>T</sup>. Its length is n−k bits. Because cH<sup>T</sup> = 0, s = (c ⊕ e)H<sup>T</sup> = eH<sup>T</sup>. The syndrome therefore names the error pattern, not the message. All error patterns that differ by a codeword give the same syndrome; such patterns form a coset.

Minimum distance decides the guarantee. A code detects up to d<sub>min</sub> − 1 errors and corrects t = ⌊(d<sub>min</sub> − 1)/2⌋ errors. For correction, build a syndrome table: list each correctable error pattern e and its syndrome s = eH<sup>T</sup>. On reception compute s, look up e, and output r ⊕ e. If s = 0, accept r as a codeword.

The standard array is the same idea in one line: write all 2<sup>k</sup> codewords in the first row, then add the most likely error pattern (coset leader) to every codeword of that row, and repeat for every coset. The decoder finds r in the array and reads the top entry of its column.

Hardware follows the algebra. The encoder XORs together the rows of G picked out by the 1 bits of m; bit j of the codeword is the modulo-2 sum of the entries in column j of those rows. In systematic form the first k bits are wires and only the n − k parity bits need XOR gates. The syndrome calculator is n − k XOR trees, one per row of H; each tree adds the received bits where that row of H has a 1. A small table (a read-only memory) maps the syndrome to the error pattern.

The Hamming (7,4) code has n = 7, k = 4 and n − k = 3 parity bits. Its H has as columns all seven nonzero 3-bit words. With G = [I₄ | P] and P rows 110, 101, 011, 111, the matrix H = [P<sup>T</sup> | I₃] has columns 110, 101, 011, 111, 100, 010, 001, in that order. No column is zero and no two columns are equal, so no single error gives s = 0 and no two single errors share a syndrome. Listing all 16 codewords confirms it: one has weight 0, seven have weight 3, seven have weight 4 and one (1111111) has weight 7, so d<sub>min</sub> = 3 and t = 1.

The Hamming bound for t = 1 is 2<sup>n−k</sup> ≥ 1 + n. For (7,4): 2<sup>3</sup> = 8 and 1 + 7 = 8. The bound is met exactly, so the code is perfect: every one of the eight syndromes is used, one for no error and seven for the seven single-bit errors. It corrects one error in seven bits with only three parity bits.

Decoding is direct. Compute s. If s = 000, no correction. Otherwise s equals one column of H; flip the bit at that column position. For example, s = 111 is column 4 in the H above, so the error is 0001000. This is why the syndrome must not be read as a decimal position: 111 is binary 7, but here it means bit 4. The column order in H sets the table.

figure.caption: Worked example 1 bit by bit: 1011 encodes to 1011010, the channel flips bit 4, and the syndrome 111 equals column 4 of H, which names the wrong bit; flipping it back restores the codeword.

spec.aria: Rows of bit cells numbered 1 to 7: message 1011, codeword 1011010, received 1010010 with bit 4 highlighted. Below, the seven columns of H, 110, 101, 011, 111, 100, 010, 001, with column 4 highlighted as matching the syndrome 111. Last row: the corrected word 1011010.

examples.question: For the (7,4) Hamming code take G = [I₄ | P] with rows of P equal to 110, 101, 011 and 111. (a) Encode m = 1011. (b) Flip the fourth bit of the codeword and decode it by syndrome.
steps: m = 1011 selects rows 1, 3 and 4 because its four bits are 1, 0, 1, 1.
Add the selected rows modulo 2: r1 ⊕ r3 = 1010101; then 1010101 ⊕ r4 = 1011010. So c = 1011010.
The parity-check matrix is H = [P<sup>T</sup> | I₃], with rows 1101100, 1011010, 0111001. Its columns are 110, 101, 011, 111, 100, 010, 001.
Flip bit 4 of c. c = 1 0 1 1 0 1 0 becomes r = 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 = 1010010. The error is e = 0001000.
Column 4 of H is 111. The table therefore gives e = 0001000.
Correct: r ⊕ e = 1010010 ⊕ 0001000 = 1011010, the original codeword.
examples.answer: The codeword is c = 1011010; after one bit flip r = 1010010, the syndrome is s = 111 (bits 1, 1, 1), the error is 0001000, and the corrected word is 1011010.

traps: Reading the syndrome as a decimal error position. In the (7,4) example 111 is a 3-bit column label; it points to column 4 because of the chosen H, not to bit 7.
Forgetting that d<sub>min</sub> = 3 detects two errors but corrects only one. A two-bit error can land on a syndrome that the table maps to a single-bit pattern, so the decoder may miscorrect.
Mixing the blocks in G and H. Systematic G is [I<sub>k</sub> | P], not [P | I<sub>k</sub>]; H is [P<sup>T</sup> | I<sub>n−k</sub>]. Swapping them breaks GH<sup>T</sup> = 0.
Using a different column order in H than the one used to build the syndrome table. The syndrome is only a pointer to that table.

quiz.q: Define an (n,k) code, code rate, and Hamming weight.
quiz.a: An (n,k) code maps k message bits to n codeword bits. Code rate is k/n. Hamming weight is the number of 1 bits in a word.

quiz.q: Why does the syndrome depend only on the error pattern and not on the transmitted codeword?
quiz.a: s = rH<sup>T</sup> = (c ⊕ e)H<sup>T</sup> = cH<sup>T</sup> ⊕ eH<sup>T</sup>. Every codeword has cH<sup>T</sup> = 0, so s = eH<sup>T</sup>.

quiz.q: For the (7,4) H in the example, r = 1101011. Find the syndrome and the corrected word.
A code has d<sub>min</sub> = 5. How many errors can it detect and correct?
quiz.a: It detects up to d<sub>min</sub> − 1 = 4 errors. It corrects t = ⌊(5 − 1)/2⌋ = 2 errors.

quiz.q: For G = [I₄ | P] with P rows 110, 101, 011, 111, write H.
Why is the (7,4) Hamming code called perfect?
quiz.a: For t = 1, the Hamming bound gives 2<sup>3</sup> ≥ 1 + 7, and 8 = 8. All eight syndromes are used by no error or one of seven single-bit errors, so no syndrome is wasted.

beyond: Not for the exam. Hamming codes appear in ECC memory as SECDED, single-error correction with double-error detection, usually an extended Hamming code with one extra parity bit. The same syndrome idea scales to BCH, Reed-Solomon and LDPC decoders, where the check matrix is sparse or polynomial-based. Search for SECDED, syndrome decoding, and parity-check matrix to go further.
